questions.stem: Under IAS 7, what are the three sections of the statement of cash flows?
options: Operating, investing and financing activities
Revenue, expenses and profit
Assets, liabilities and equity
Current, non-current and contingent items
questions.why: IAS 7 requires cash flows to be classified into operating, investing and financing activities.
whyNot: Those are elements of the statement of comprehensive income.
Those are elements of the statement of financial position.
That is not a classification used in IAS 7.

questions.stem: How is depreciation treated in the statement of cash flows?
options: Added back to operating profit, because no cash left the business
Deducted from operating profit, because it is an expense
Shown under investing activities
Excluded entirely, with no adjustment made
questions.why: Depreciation reduced profit without any movement of cash, so it must be added back to arrive at cash generated from operations.
whyNot: It was already deducted in arriving at operating profit.
Investing activities show the cash cost of buying assets, not depreciation.
An adjustment is essential, because the statement starts from operating profit.

questions.stem: Inventory has increased over the year. What is the effect in the statement of cash flows?
options: A negative adjustment, because cash has been spent on stock
A positive adjustment, because stock is an asset
No adjustment, because inventory is not cash
It is shown under investing activities
questions.why: Cash moves in the opposite direction to an asset: more inventory means cash has been used.
whyNot: Holding more of an asset consumes cash rather than providing it.
The whole purpose of the working capital adjustments is to convert profit into cash.
Inventory is part of working capital, within operating activities.

questions.stem: Trade payables have increased over the year. What is the effect?
options: A positive adjustment, because suppliers have not yet been paid
A negative adjustment, because the company owes more
No adjustment, because payables are not cash
It is shown under financing activities
questions.why: Cash moves in the same direction as a liability: more credit from suppliers means cash has been retained.
whyNot: Owing more means less cash has gone out this year.
Payables are part of the working capital adjustment.
Trade payables are an operating item, not financing.

questions.stem: Where are dividends paid shown?
options: Under financing activities
Under operating activities
Under investing activities
They are not shown at all
questions.why: Dividends paid are a return to the providers of equity finance, so they belong in financing activities.
whyNot: Interest paid is shown within operating activities, but dividends are not.
Investing activities concern non-current assets and investments.
They are a real cash outflow and must be shown.

questions.stem: A profit on disposal of a non-current asset of $9,000 is included in operating profit. How is it treated?
options: Deducted, because the full proceeds appear under investing activities
Added back, because it is a non-cash gain
Ignored, because it is included in profit already
Shown as a financing inflow
questions.why: The whole of the cash received appears separately under investing activities, so leaving the profit in operating would double count it.
whyNot: A loss on disposal is added back; a profit is deducted.
Leaving it in would overstate operating cash flow.
Disposal proceeds are an investing inflow, not financing.

questions.stem: Operating profit is $210,000, depreciation $85,000, profit on disposal $9,000, inventory up $56,000, receivables up $57,000 and payables up $12,000. What is cash generated from operations?
whyNot: That adds the profit on disposal instead of deducting it.
That deducts the increase in payables instead of adding it.
That omits the working capital movements entirely.

questions.stem: Opening cash was $26,000 and net cash flow for the year was an outflow of $11,000. What is closing cash?
questions.why: 26,000 - 11,000 = $15,000, which must agree with the cash figure in the statement of financial position.
whyNot: That adds the outflow instead of deducting it.
That ignores the opening balance.
That is the opening balance.

questions.stem: A share issue raises $200,000, of which $80,000 is share premium. What appears under financing activities?
options: $200,000, because the premium is cash too
$120,000, being the nominal value only
$80,000, being the premium only
Nothing, because a share issue is not a cash flow
questions.why: The statement records cash, so the whole of the proceeds is shown regardless of how it is split within equity.
whyNot: Including only the nominal value understates the cash raised.
The premium alone is not the total received.
A share issue for cash is a financing inflow.

questions.stem: Which of the following appears under investing activities?
options: Proceeds from the sale of a delivery vehicle
Interest paid on a debenture
Repayment of a bank loan
An increase in trade receivables
questions.why: Investing activities cover cash flows from buying and selling non-current assets and investments.
whyNot: Interest paid is shown within operating activities.
Loan repayment is a financing outflow.
That is a working capital movement within operating activities.

questions.stem: Why can a profitable company still run out of cash?
options: Profit is recognised when a sale is made, while the cash may arrive much later
Profit figures are always inaccurate
Cash is not recorded in the accounting system
Profit includes only cash transactions
questions.why: The gap between profit and cash comes from credit sales, inventory build-up, capital spending and non-cash charges.
whyNot: Audited profit is reasonably reliable; the issue is timing.
Cash is recorded fully; the point is that it differs from profit.
Profit includes credit transactions, which is exactly the problem.

questions.stem: A company bought $260,000 of equipment and raised only $150,000 of long-term finance. What does this indicate?
options: A financing mismatch: long-term investment funded partly out of short-term resources
That the company is over-capitalised
That the company has made a loss
That the equipment was bought at the wrong price
questions.why: Long-term assets should be funded by long-term finance, and naming the mismatch is what earns the evaluation marks.
whyNot: Over-capitalisation means holding too much long-term finance, which is the opposite.
Cash flow says nothing directly about whether a loss was made.
The issue is how it was funded, not what it cost.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines overtrading?
options: Expanding sales faster than the working capital available to support them
Selling goods below their cost price
Trading in more countries than the company can manage
Paying dividends greater than profit for the year
questions.why: Rapid growth consumes cash, because inventory and receivables grow with sales while the cash to fund them must come from somewhere.
whyNot: That is loss-making pricing, a different problem.
That is over-expansion, not overtrading in the technical sense.
That is an uncovered dividend.

questions.stem: Which of the following positive cash flows is least likely to be repeatable?
options: Proceeds from selling non-current assets
Cash generated from operations
A reduction in receivables days achieved by better credit control
An increase in sales volume
questions.why: Asset sales cannot be repeated each year, and they often shrink the capacity to earn, so distinguishing them from trading cash flow is essential.
whyNot: Operating cash flow is the recurring source and the one that matters most.
A sustained improvement in credit control has a lasting effect on the level of receivables.
Higher sales volume can continue, though growth also consumes cash.

questions.stem: Why is cash flow information often considered more reliable than profit?
options: Cash received and paid is a matter of record, while profit depends on accounting judgements
Cash flow statements are audited and profit statements are not
Cash flow includes forecasts, while profit does not
Cash flow is not affected by the level of sales
questions.why: Profit depends on judgements about depreciation, inventory valuation and provisions, whereas cash movements are factual.
whyNot: Both statements are covered by the audit.
Neither statement contains forecasts; a cash budget does.
Cash flow is heavily affected by sales and how they are collected.

questions.stem: Net book value of an asset disposed of was $25,000 and the proceeds were $34,000. What appears where?
options: A profit of $9,000 deducted in operating activities and $34,000 added in investing activities
A profit of $9,000 added in operating activities and $25,000 in investing activities
$25,000 in investing activities only
$34,000 deducted in investing activities
questions.why: The cash received is $34,000, and the $9,000 profit already in operating profit must be removed to avoid double counting.
whyNot: A profit on disposal is deducted, and the cash shown is the proceeds.
The net book value is not a cash flow.
Proceeds are an inflow, not an outflow.

questions.stem: Interest paid during the year is shown:
options: Within operating activities, after cash generated from operations
Within financing activities, alongside dividends paid
Within investing activities
As an adjustment added back to operating profit
questions.why: IAS 7 as applied in this specification shows interest paid within operating activities, after cash generated from operations.
whyNot: Dividends paid are financing; interest paid is operating in this layout.
Investing activities concern non-current assets.
It is a genuine cash outflow, not a non-cash adjustment.

questions.stem: Which figure must the statement of cash flows reconcile to?
options: The closing cash balance in the statement of financial position
The profit for the year
The total of non-current assets
The closing balance of retained earnings
questions.why: Opening cash plus the net change must equal closing cash, and that is the first check to apply.
whyNot: Profit and cash differ, which is the purpose of the statement.
Non-current assets are only part of the investing section.
Retained earnings is reconciled in the statement of changes in equity.

questions.stem: Why does a company's liquidity matter more than its profit in the short term?
options: A company fails when it cannot pay what it owes, whatever its reported profit
Profit is not important to any stakeholder
Liquidity determines the level of taxation payable
Lenders do not look at profit
questions.why: Wages, suppliers and interest have to be paid in cash, and a supplier who is not paid stops supplying.
whyNot: Profit matters greatly over the longer term.
Tax is based on profit, not liquidity.
Lenders look at both, with particular attention to the ability to service the debt.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of the statement of cash flows?
options: It is historical and contains no forecast, so a cash budget is needed to look ahead
It cannot be prepared from published financial statements
It excludes all capital expenditure
It is not required by accounting standards
questions.why: It explains why cash moved in a period that has ended, and a single year can be distorted by timing around the year end.
whyNot: It is prepared from the two statements of financial position and the income statement.
Capital expenditure appears under investing activities.
IAS 7 requires it.
